slides.head: Welcome to Principals
points: A board game played on your phone
slides.say: Welcome to Principals. In this game you sit on a company board, and the board has to decide what to tell the public and what to do about a real problem. You play on your phone. The projector shows the room how everyone is doing. This video covers the rules in about five minutes, so you know what to expect before we start.

slides.head: Join on your phone
points: Open the link or scan the code
slides.say: First, join. Open the link your professor shares, or scan the code on the screen. Type the game code and your name, then tap Join.

slides.head: Wait for your seat
points: You land in the waiting room
Boards and roles appear on your phone
slides.say: You wait in the waiting room until your professor places you. The host can assign everyone by hand, or let the game do it automatically. When you are placed, your phone shows your board and your role. Most of you will sit on one of five company boards. A few of you will play outside the boards, and I will get to that role in a minute.

slides.head: You get a private role card
slides.say: Every director gets a private role card. It says who you are on the board, like the attorney, a labor director, or the fund partner. It also gives you a motive, a reason you might want to keep quiet. The card shows a goal that earns points, and a penalty if things go badly. Nobody else sees your card. Your interests will not always match the board's interests, and that is the point.

slides.head: Every board has a problem
points: There is a case for silence
slides.say: Each round, your board gets a problem to deal with. A short briefing tells you what is going on, and it is uncertain on purpose. Maybe a report is still a draft. Maybe the numbers are disputed. Under the briefing is the case for staying silent. It is a real argument, and a tempting one.

slides.head: Vote on which facts to tell
points: Switch on the facts you would admit
Bars show how bad each fact is
slides.say: Next, the board votes on which facts to admit. Each fact has a switch. Bars show how bad the fact looks if it comes out, and the facts that look worst are also the easiest for others to find. Telling a fact costs the share price a small fee. Hiding it is free, until someone finds it. Each director votes, and the facts with the most votes get told. The Chair locks the result.

slides.head: Write one public statement
points: It is printed in the newspaper
Pick a line or write your own
slides.say: Then the board agrees on one public statement. The newspaper prints it as the board's quote, so choose your words with care. You can pick a ready-made line or write your own. Talk it through in the board chat, then the Chair calls the vote.

slides.head: One headline vote per round
points: Arrows show who gains and loses
slides.say: Now the big decision. Each round, your board votes on one headline motion. It is a plain yes or no. Five small icons show who it helps and who it hurts: owners, workers, customers, the community, and the public. An up arrow means they gain, and a down arrow means they lose. You will not see numbers, only arrows. The Chair calls the vote, and a motion passes if there are more yes votes than no.

slides.head: Two rounds, eight minutes each
points: A timer runs on your phone
slides.say: The game has two rounds, and each round runs about eight minutes. Round one is The Warning. Round two is The Hard Choice. A timer shows on your phone. If your board cannot decide in time, that is a result too, and the newspaper will say so.

slides.head: The Auditor plays outside
points: Your goal is to be credible
slides.say: A few students play the Auditor, from outside the boards. Each round, you choose one board to inspect. If that board hid a fact, you may find it. The Auditor has a goal of their own too, so choose carefully. The Auditor is how hiding gets punished, and it is played by your classmates.

slides.head: The Principal Times
points: A front page for the whole room
slides.say: On the projector, you will see The Principal Times, a newspaper front page. As each board decides, its story fills in. The headline comes from the motion result. Little squares show how much of the story the board told. The statement appears as a quote, and the share price moves. When the Auditor or the press catches a hidden fact, it prints in red under the story.

slides.head: How you score
points: Up to plus 15 if your board does well
slides.say: Here is how you score. If you reach the goal on your card, you earn fifty points. If you fall into the penalty on your card, you lose thirty five. And you can earn up to fifteen more points when your board does well for the group you care about. You can do well even when your board does not, so read your card carefully.

slides.head: Reveal and debrief
points: The projector tells each board story
slides.say: At the end, your phone shows your own result. Then the projector walks through each board: what it said in public, what it left out, and what really happened in cases like it. Then we talk. Heads up, together. That is where the learning happens.

slides.head: What to remember
slides.say: So, to remember. Read your card. Talk with your board. Vote on the facts, write the statement, then vote on the motion. And have fun with it. See you in class.
